reading.title: How to Build a Fair Argument
reading.purpose: Learn the steps that make a speech or an essay fair and strong.
paras: In everyday talk, an argument can mean an angry quarrel between friends. In school, the word has a calmer meaning. An argument is a set of reasons that supports an idea. When students debate, they take turns giving reasons instead of raising their voices.

Every strong argument starts with a viewpoint, the way you think about a topic. Suppose you believe recess should be longer. That is your viewpoint, but it will not change anyone's mind alone. You also need proof, such as facts, numbers, or a report from a reliable source.

Next, make sure your reasons are logical. Each step should follow from the one before it. For example, "Longer recess helps students focus, so everyone will get perfect scores" is not logical, because the second part does not follow from the first. Also choose sources that are trustworthy, such as a school nurse or a careful study, rather than a rumor.

A fair speaker looks at the whole question. If you tell only one side, your talk is one-sided, and listeners may stop trusting you. Use a phrase such as on the other hand to show that you have thought about a different view, then explain why your reasons are still stronger. When your proof is clear, your talk will be convincing, which means listeners will believe it.
End with a short summary. Begin it with in conclusion, then repeat your viewpoint and your best proof in one or two sentences. A calm, fair ending shows respect for the topic and for your audience.

qs.q: In paragraph 1, the word "argument" is used to mean
choices: an angry quarrel between two friends over a game
a set of reasons that supports an idea
a short summary at the end of a talk
a fact taken from a reliable report
qs.why: The writer first names the everyday meaning, then says that in school an argument is "a set of reasons that supports an idea."

qs.q: Which sentence tells how to check that reasons are logical?
choices: You also need proof, such as facts, numbers, or a report from a reliable source.
A fair speaker looks at the whole question.
Each step should follow from the one before it.
qs.why: This sentence gives the test: a logical reason follows from the step before it.

ev.text: Each step should follow from the one before it.

qs.q: Why might listeners stop trusting a speaker whose talk is one-sided?
choices: They may feel the speaker used far too many facts to prove a single point.
They may think the speaker talked longer than the rules allow.
They may notice the speaker said in conclusion before the end.
They may sense the speaker ignored a different view of the question.
qs.why: A talk that tells only one side leaves out the other views, and listeners can tell something is missing.

qs.q: What is the main idea of this reading?
choices: A good argument joins a clear viewpoint with proof and fair thinking.
A debate is won by the student who speaks the loudest and the longest.
Only experts are allowed to share a viewpoint in school.
A talk must always begin with the phrase in conclusion.
qs.why: Each paragraph adds one step: a viewpoint, proof, logical reasons, fairness, and a summary.
